messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan Mercer was 33 when he came for treatment, a married federal prosecutor who had built his career on being composed, precise, and hard to shake. The attack happened nine months earlier, on a weekday afternoon at the downtown courthouse complex where he worked. He had gone downstairs between hearings to meet a witness liaison near the public entrance. He remembered the smell first, though even now he could not place it neatly in sequence: a sharp alcoholic odor from a man weaving near the security line, something sour on his breath as he argued with a guard. After that, the story broke apart. There was a bang that did not immediately register as an explosion, then another sound and a pressure wave that seemed to hit his chest and ears at once. People dropped, glass burst inward, and the lobby became a blur of dust, alarms, and shouting. What stayed with him most was the conviction, formed in an instant, that he should have moved faster, shouted sooner, done something to get people back. He had helped after the blast, but in his mind that fact never carried the same weight as the seconds before it.

In the months after, Ethan found that he could not tell a clear story of what had happened, even to himself. When he tried, he got stuck on fragments: the alcohol smell, a woman’s shoe on the floor, the concussive bang, the sense that time had narrowed. The memories did not feel like ordinary recollections that could be reviewed and set down. They came with a force that made them feel more real than the rest of his day, as if the courthouse lobby were suddenly overlaying the room he was actually in. At those moments it did not seem past at all; it felt current, immediate, as though his body had not understood that the blast was over.

What frightened Ethan almost as much as the attack was what he had come to believe it said about him. He was certain that he had failed in a basic duty to protect other people, and he repeated to himself that he would never forgive his own inaction. Working as a prosecutor had once rested on a broad confidence in institutions and in other people’s stated intentions. Since the bombing, that had narrowed into suspicion. He watched faces in courthouse elevators, studied hands and coats in hallways, and felt convinced that people were not what they seemed. Those beliefs sharpened whenever he was jolted by reminders of the attack. On mornings after late-night trial preparation, when he came to work exhausted and mentally thin, he was harsher with himself and more certain that his fatigue proved he would miss warning signs again. If someone passed him in the courthouse corridor smelling of liquor or mouthwash, his stomach dropped and his mind went straight back to the man near security; in the same instant he was flooded with the thought that he should have recognized danger and failed. A slammed file drawer or a construction bang outside chambers could make him scan the floor plan for exits while privately condemning himself for trusting anyone around him.

Those appraisals seemed to pull the memories closer rather than settle them. The more Ethan interrogated himself about the seconds before the blast—what he should have noticed, whether a better prosecutor, a better man, would have prevented it—the less coherent the event became. He would sit at home trying to explain it to his wife and instead get seized by vivid shards that felt as if they were happening in his living room. He was not reviewing the attack so much as being dropped back inside it, with the same sensory force and the same absence of sequence. And once the memory arrived in that immediate, overreal way, it deepened the verdict he had already reached: if the scene still felt this alive, then to him it meant the failure was not finished, not absolved, and that he remained the man who had not protected people when it counted.

That loop had begun to shape his work and marriage. At the courthouse he timed his movements to avoid the public entrance where the bombing occurred, taking a longer route through secured staff corridors whenever he could. He hated how deliberate this had become, because it confirmed his sense that the world was full of concealed threat and that he could not trust himself to manage it. When he was tired, the memories came more easily and the day felt dangerous from the outset; once a memory had been stirred up, even routine noises or a trace of alcohol on someone’s breath seemed primed to set him off again. His wife told him he looked perpetually braced, and he admitted that he no longer believed he could read people accurately. He sought help after freezing in court when a loud bang from nearby construction made the courtroom disappear and the lobby come back with full force. What brought him in was not only the fear of another episode in public, but the deeper conviction underneath it: that if he could not make sense of what happened, he would remain the man who failed others, and that any lapse—especially when tired—could mean he would fail them again.
